label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Jess, I know what you meant.

When you texted last night that it was one assignment and I shouldn’t torch my job over it, I didn’t hear “stop caring.” I heard a friend who knows what schools can do to people who become inconvenient. We met student teaching in 2012. You’ve seen me care too much about things that did not deserve a Sunday afternoon, much less a professional consequence. You’re allowed to ask whether this is one of those things.

And since half the group chat apparently shares your concern, here is my attempt to answer without making everyone’s phone buzz through dinner.

For anyone who missed the beginning: I teach two sections of juniors in US History II at Cobb Street High. For the past four years, I’ve assigned an oral history project about Boston’s busing and desegregation fight in 1974–76. Students interview someone in their family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, and write a two-page reflection.

This year, a parent emailed Dr. Halvorsen, copied a school committee member, and said the assignment “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.”

Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. We’re meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I don’t plan to drop it.

But I need to say something before explaining why: I think the parent has a point.

Not about whether we should teach this history. About the pressure.

An assignment handed out by a teacher is not a casual invitation, however pleasantly I explain it. There’s a grade attached. Some students will hear “interview someone in your family” and think they’re supposed to come back with a revelation. Some will feel responsible for whatever a relative says. Some may have very good reasons not to ask questions at home that I know nothing about.

I don’t want a teenager sitting across from a grandparent thinking their history grade depends on getting that person to confess something. If the assignment has left room for that understanding, I need to fix it. Four years without a complaint doesn’t prove everyone was fine.

So I’m going to keep the project and add a clear alternative. Students can interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody has to interview a family member. The options need to count equally, and choosing one shouldn’t require a student to explain their home life to me.

That’s a change I’m willing to make. More than willing. I wish I’d made it sooner.

What I’m not willing to do is treat the complaint as proof that the subject itself should go away.

This is the history of the city these kids live in. Their families lived through it. The places in the photographs are places they recognize. And the textbook gives it one paragraph.

A paragraph can tell them that desegregation happened, that there was resistance, that there was violence. It can’t do much with the fact that people they love may have been involved, or afraid, or harmed, or wrong. It certainly can’t answer the questions they have once they realize how close this history is.

In 2023, one student interviewed his grandmother, who had driven a school bus in South Boston in 1974. She’d never told anyone in the family about it. He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class.

When it stopped, nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute.

I’m a high-school teacher. I know the difference between a room that’s listening and a room that’s waiting for you to finish. They were listening.

I don’t want to make that moment carry more than it can. I can’t tell you it changed everybody’s life. I can tell you that, for those forty seconds, this wasn’t a paragraph about some people a long time ago. It was someone’s grandmother, talking about a job she’d done in their city. They had to take that in.

Last year, a student learned that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus.

She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

I’m putting those facts next to each other carefully, because her being upset was not what made the assignment good. I didn’t need her to have a painful discovery so I could feel like an effective teacher. She was a kid dealing with something she hadn’t known about someone in her family, and she deserved time and care.

What made her writing so good was how seriously she thought about it. She didn’t pretend it hadn’t happened, and she didn’t reduce her uncle’s entire life to the thing she’d learned. She tried to work out what it meant to know this about him. That’s difficult work for an adult. She was doing it honestly.

I’ve caught myself thinking that the students who are most uncomfortable with this history are the ones who need the assignment most. There’s something in that thought I still believe: discomfort isn’t always a sign that learning has gone wrong.

But it’s also a dangerously convenient thought for a teacher. It lets me decide that a student’s distress proves I’m doing something important. I don’t get to do that. I don’t get to force anyone into a family conversation and then congratulate myself for challenging them.

That’s the line I’m trying to hold. We can study hard things without requiring students to expose their families. We can make room for discomfort without treating it as the goal.

Which brings me back to your text.

You’re right that I could get burned. I’ve had tenure since 2021, so I’m not in the position of someone who can simply be told not to come back next fall. But Halvorsen still controls my schedule. He still decides who gets AP. There are plenty of ways for this to make my working life worse without becoming a story anyone else would recognize as retaliation.

I know that. I’m a little scared of it.

I’d love to report that I’m serenely certain and prepared to accept whatever comes. Mostly I’m thinking about Thursday’s meeting at inconvenient times and wondering whether I’ll explain myself well or get defensive.

I’m not going in to pick a fight with the parent. “Reopens wounds” isn’t a ridiculous concern. For some families, these aren’t settled memories. I want to hear what she’s worried about, and I want her to hear that I’m taking the pressure seriously.

But quietly dropping the project would leave the wrong thing intact. It would remove the questions rather than improve the way I’m asking students to approach them. We’d be back to the paragraph, with all the complicated parts safely outside the classroom.

I don’t think that would be a better way to teach this.

That’s my reason. Not that every assignment is a hill worth dying on, or that backing down always means failing your students. You know I’ve changed assignments, abandoned ideas, and occasionally realized halfway through a lesson that it was a complete dud. I’m capable of letting something go.

This one is worth revising and keeping.

You don’t have to agree. I mean that. I’d like you to understand why I’m doing it, but I’m not asking you to stop worrying about me. You’ve known me too long for that to be a realistic request.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. You can ask how it went before telling me whether I should’ve listened to you.
